topics.title: Iron: Why intake and absorption differ
takeaways: Heme and non-heme iron follow different absorption pathways; iron stores help regulate how much enters the body.
Vitamin C can enhance non-heme iron absorption, while some meal components inhibit it; effects in single meals need not predict long-term iron status.
Published dietary absorption estimates depend on assumptions about iron stores and diet composition, rather than describing everyone’s absorption.
Alternate-day dosing experiments in iron-depleted women measured absorption; they do not establish a universal supplement schedule.

topics.title: The luteal phase: Hormones, variation and evidence
takeaways: An app-based study of over 600,000 ovulatory cycles found a mean luteal phase of about 12 days; its selected users do not represent every population.
Progesterone raises basal body temperature after ovulation, providing one clue to cycle timing.
Reported sleep symptoms and measured sleep architecture are different outcomes; changes before menstruation are not identical for everyone.
A calcium trial studied people with clinically significant PMS. Its result does not mean everyone needs calcium supplements.

topics.title: Doomscrolling: Negative news and distress
takeaways: A broad psychology review describes stronger effects of negative than positive information across several domains; that is background evidence, not a test of a particular app.
Following the Boston Marathon bombing, heavier media exposure was associated with greater acute stress in a survey.
The Doomscrolling Scale study reports associations with personality, distress and wellbeing; the authors are Satici and colleagues.
An association can reflect several directions of influence, including distressed people seeking more news.

topics.title: Stoicism: What is up to us?
takeaways: Epictetus places judgment and moral choice at the center of what is up to us.
External outcomes can matter practically without determining whether a choice is virtuous.
Stoic accounts connect emotions to judgments; the aim is thoughtful evaluation rather than simply suppressing feelings.
The Enchiridion and Meditations are primary texts; translations and historical context affect how their language is understood.

topics.title: Inflation: Prices and purchasing power
takeaways: A price index combines many prices with weights; inflation does not mean every item rises at the same rate.
With nominal return n and inflation i, the real return is (1+n)/(1+i)-1; subtraction is an approximation.
A wage increase below the inflation rate lowers purchasing power relative to that price index.
Friedman’s 1968 monetary-policy argument is historical scholarship, not a complete explanation of every inflation episode.

topics.title: Scaling laws: Patterns and limits
takeaways: Kaplan and colleagues reported power-law relationships within the training regimes they studied.
The Chinchilla study showed that compute allocation between model size and training data matters.
Its often cited tokens-per-parameter ratio comes from a particular optimization study, rather than a permanent prescription.
Schaeffer and colleagues show that apparent emergence can depend on the evaluation metric.

topics.title: GDPR: Understanding the right of access
takeaways: Article 15 covers a copy of personal data and information such as purposes, recipients and retention.
Access requests are generally free; identification and narrowly defined exceptions can affect the response.
The normal response period is one month. An extension of two further months requires justification and notice within the first month.
Access is not unlimited: other people’s rights and specific legal restrictions may matter.

topics.title: Circadian rhythms: How light changes timing
takeaways: The suprachiasmatic nucleus helps coordinate daily rhythms across the body.
Light can advance or delay circadian phase depending on when it occurs relative to the internal clock.
Experiments on natural light exposure and evening light-emitting readers test specific conditions, rather than universal routines.
Molecular clock mechanisms explain recurring rhythms; sleep timing also depends on sleep pressure and circumstances.

topics.title: Interrupted work: Attention and resuming a task
takeaways: Leroy and Glomb tested interruptions involving anticipated time pressure when resuming work.
A ready-to-resume plan reduced the measured attention costs in their experiments; the result is context dependent.
In Mark and colleagues’ experiment, interrupted participants compensated with faster work while reporting more stress.
Speed, accuracy and experienced strain are separate outcomes, so one measure cannot describe the whole cost.

topics.title: Ego depletion: A theory tested by replication
takeaways: The 1998 paper introduced experimental evidence for a limited-resource account of self-control.
A 2016 replication across 23 laboratories found an effect near zero for its specified protocol.
Job and colleagues studied how beliefs about willpower interact with performance; this does not settle every competing explanation.
A failed replication challenges a tested claim without proving that fatigue or motivation never matters.

topics.title: Index funds: Benchmarks, costs and comparison
takeaways: Sharpe’s arithmetic compares active and passive dollars within the same market under explicitly stated definitions.
His discussion also notes sampling, fees and misleading benchmark comparisons; an index fund need not own every security.
Fama–French and Carhart studied historical mutual-fund performance, including costs and the difficulty of separating persistence from luck.
Index tracking does not remove market risk, and a narrow index does not provide broad diversification.

topics.title: The gut–brain axis: Mechanisms and evidence
takeaways: The enteric nervous system participates in gut function and communicates with the central nervous system.
Gut-produced serotonin and brain serotonin are distinct pools; a simple increase in one does not imply an increase in the other.
Sudo and colleagues’ stress-response experiment involved germ-free mice, not a demonstrated treatment in humans.
Valles-Colomer and colleagues found human microbiome associations with quality of life and depression; associations alone cannot establish causation.

topics.title: Glucose and fructose: Two sugars, different routes
takeaways: Glucose and fructose are monosaccharides; sucrose combines one of each.
Their intestinal transport and initial metabolic steps differ.
Food structure, quantity and the overall diet matter when interpreting metabolic effects.

topics.title: ATP: How cells pay for their work
takeaways: ATP couples energy-releasing reactions to energy-requiring processes.
Glycolysis and mitochondrial metabolism contribute to ATP production.
Cells continually regenerate ATP rather than storing a lifetime supply.

topics.title: Insulin and glucagon: Keeping fuel available
takeaways: Pancreatic beta cells release insulin; alpha cells release glucagon.
Insulin supports fuel uptake and storage in responsive tissues.
Glucagon helps the liver make glucose available between meals.

topics.title: Glycogen: The body’s carbohydrate reserve
takeaways: Glycogen is a branched polymer of glucose.
Liver glycogen contributes to blood glucose regulation.
Muscle glycogen supplies fuel locally during activity.

topics.title: Dietary fat: From the intestine to your cells
takeaways: Bile helps emulsify dietary fat.
Digestive enzymes break lipids into absorbable components.
Lipoproteins transport many lipids through the circulation.

topics.title: Protein digestion: What happens after a meal
takeaways: Stomach and intestinal enzymes break proteins into smaller units.
Amino acids supply building blocks for many body proteins.
Protein synthesis and breakdown both occur throughout life.

topics.title: The liver: A chemical processing hub
takeaways: The liver processes nutrients arriving from the digestive tract.
It participates in carbohydrate, lipid and amino acid metabolism.
Metabolic processing changes molecules; it does not make every exposure harmless.

topics.title: Kidneys: Why urine is more than filtered water
takeaways: Filtration occurs at the renal corpuscle.
Tubules reabsorb useful substances and secrete others.
Final urine composition reflects several stages of regulation.

topics.title: Electrolytes: Why charged minerals matter
takeaways: Electrolytes dissociate into charged particles in solution.
Sodium and potassium are distributed differently across cell membranes.
Fluid and electrolyte regulation involves the kidneys and hormonal signals.

topics.title: Acid–base balance: How blood pH stays stable
takeaways: Buffers resist sudden changes in pH.
The lungs regulate carbon dioxide removal.
The kidneys contribute through hydrogen ion and bicarbonate handling.

topics.title: Nerve signals: Electricity made from ions
takeaways: Ion gradients and membrane permeability determine membrane potential.
Action potentials involve coordinated opening of ion channels.
Synapses transfer signals between cells through electrical or chemical mechanisms.

topics.title: Muscle contraction: From a nerve signal to movement
takeaways: Actin and myosin interact in the sliding filament mechanism.
Calcium allows contraction to be activated.
ATP supports cross-bridge cycling and relaxation processes.

topics.title: Oxygen transport: What your lungs and blood actually do
takeaways: Gas exchange depends on partial-pressure gradients.
Hemoglobin carries most oxygen in blood.
Carbon dioxide travels in several forms, including bicarbonate.

topics.title: Immunity: Fast defenses and learned responses
takeaways: Innate defenses act without the same antigen specificity as adaptive responses.
B and T lymphocytes participate in adaptive immunity.
Immunological memory changes responses to later encounters.

topics.title: Hormone receptors: Why one signal affects some cells
takeaways: A target cell needs the relevant receptor to respond.
Receptors can act at the membrane or inside the cell.
Feedback loops help regulate many endocrine pathways.

topics.title: The menstrual cycle: Coordinating ovaries and uterus
takeaways: FSH and LH help regulate ovarian activity.
Estrogen and progesterone influence the uterine lining.
Ovulation and cycle length vary; calendar dates alone do not establish hormone levels.

topics.title: Vitamin B12: What it does and how it is handled
takeaways: Vitamin B12 contributes to DNA synthesis and neurological function.
Normal absorption involves intrinsic factor and the small intestine.
Low intake and impaired absorption are distinct causes of deficiency.

topics.title: Vitamin D: What it does and how it is handled
takeaways: Vitamin D undergoes activation steps in the body.
It helps regulate calcium absorption and bone health.
Requirements and safe intake limits are different measures.

topics.title: Vitamin C: What it does and how it is handled
takeaways: Vitamin C supports collagen synthesis.

topics.title: Vitamin B1: What it does and how it is handled
takeaways: Thiamin is a water-soluble vitamin.

topics.title: Vitamin A: What it does and how it is handled
takeaways: Retinal participates in the visual cycle.
Retinoids contribute to cell differentiation.
Preformed vitamin A and provitamin A carotenoids have different intake considerations.

topics.title: Vitamin K: What it does and how it is handled
takeaways: Vitamin K supports activation of several clotting-related proteins.
It also has roles in bone-related proteins.

topics.title: Bonds: What you own when you lend money
takeaways: The issuer borrows; the bondholder lends.
Coupon, maturity and principal define core promised cash flows.
Credit risk concerns the issuer’s ability to meet its obligations.

topics.title: Bond prices: Why rising rates can reduce value
takeaways: Bond prices reflect the present value of future cash flows.
For fixed-rate bonds, higher required yields generally mean lower prices.
Maturity and cash-flow timing affect sensitivity to interest-rate changes.

topics.title: Bond yield: Why a coupon is not your return
takeaways: Coupon rate describes interest relative to face value.
Current yield relates annual interest to market price.
Yield to maturity depends on assumptions and does not guarantee realized returns.

topics.title: Bond risk: Credit, inflation and early repayment
takeaways: Inflation can erode the purchasing power of payments.
Selling before maturity exposes the holder to market prices.
Callable bonds may be repaid early under their terms.

topics.title: Marketing: Finding a need worth serving
takeaways: Customer needs guide the offer.
Value includes perceived benefits and the costs of obtaining them.
A marketing strategy connects the offer to a chosen audience.

topics.title: Consumer behavior: How purchase decisions happen
takeaways: Need recognition can start a purchase process.
People search for information and evaluate alternatives.
Experience after purchase influences future decisions.

topics.title: Segmentation: Which customers share a useful need?
takeaways: Segmentation groups customers using relevant differences.
A segment should support actionable marketing decisions.
A demographic label alone does not explain a customer’s needs.

topics.title: Positioning: The comparison customers make
takeaways: Positioning depends on a target audience and competing alternatives.
A meaningful difference must matter to that audience.
Communication and product experience need to support the same promise.

topics.title: Marketing research: Asking questions that change decisions
takeaways: Begin with a defined problem.
Qualitative and quantitative methods answer different kinds of questions.
Sampling and measurement choices limit what findings can support.

topics.title: Pricing: What a number communicates
takeaways: Costs help establish the economics of an offer.
Customers compare price with perceived value and alternatives.
A pricing objective should be explicit before choosing a tactic.

topics.title: Branding: Building expectations people remember
takeaways: Brand identity and customer perception are related but distinct.
Brands help customers recognize and compare offers.
Experience can strengthen or weaken communicated promises.

topics.title: Marketing ethics: Persuasion, evidence and trust
takeaways: Claims should have appropriate support.
Customers need material information to evaluate an offer.
Ethical evaluation includes the consequences of marketing choices.

topics.title: Retrieval practice: Why remembering is part of learning
takeaways: Practice recalling before checking the answer.
Feedback helps identify omissions and errors.
Recall questions should test understanding as well as isolated facts.

topics.title: Spaced practice: Making room for forgetting
takeaways: Spread study across sessions.
Use later sessions to retrieve older material.
The useful spacing interval depends on the material and the retention goal.

topics.title: Interleaving: Learning which method to choose
takeaways: Mix related kinds of problems.
Practice recognizing which strategy applies.
More difficult practice does not automatically mean poorer learning.

topics.title: Elaboration: Explaining why a fact makes sense
takeaways: Ask why and how questions.
Connect new material to prior knowledge.
Verify explanations rather than accepting a plausible story.

topics.title: Concrete examples: Giving an abstract idea something to attach to
takeaways: Find examples that instantiate the same concept.
Explain which features are relevant.
Use varied cases so understanding can transfer.

topics.title: Dual coding: Connecting words and diagrams
takeaways: Connect a visual with a verbal explanation.
Choose visuals that represent the content rather than decorate it.
Reconstructing a diagram can become retrieval practice.

topics.title: Copyright: An idea versus its expression
takeaways: Copyright generally concerns expression rather than ideas as such.
Ownership, licensing and exceptions are separate questions.
Rules and remedies depend on the applicable jurisdiction.

topics.title: Patents: Disclosure in exchange for exclusivity
takeaways: Patentability involves requirements such as novelty and inventive step.
A granted patent is territorial.
The claims define the protected subject matter.

topics.title: Trade secrets: Protecting knowledge without publishing it
takeaways: Secrecy and protective measures matter.
Trade secret protection does not generally prevent independent development.
Protection can be lost when information becomes public.

topics.title: Trademarks: Protecting the sign customers recognize
takeaways: Trademarks distinguish goods or services.
Protection relates to territory and relevant goods or services.
Distinctiveness affects whether a sign can function as a trademark.

topics.title: WTO non-discrimination: Two different comparisons
takeaways: MFN concerns treatment among trading partners.
National treatment concerns imported and domestic products under relevant rules.
Treaty scope and exceptions matter to the analysis.

topics.title: International arbitration: How an award crosses borders
takeaways: An arbitration agreement and an arbitral award perform different roles.
The New York Convention provides a framework for recognition and enforcement.
Enforcement may be refused on specified grounds; local procedure still matters.

topics.title: Electoral systems: How votes become seats
takeaways: Plurality, majority and proportional systems translate votes differently.
District design and electoral thresholds influence outcomes.
No single electoral system optimizes every democratic objective.

topics.title: Constitutions: Designing the rules of government
takeaways: Constitutions establish powers and procedures.
Rights and institutions require implementation to be effective.
Amendment rules balance adaptability and stability.

topics.title: Election administration: Who controls the count?
takeaways: An electoral management body needs a defined mandate.
Formal independence and practical autonomy are distinct.
Transparent procedures and accountability support credibility.

topics.title: Government formation: Who gets to govern after a vote?
takeaways: Constitutions define how governments take office.
Confidence procedures shape relationships with legislatures.
Removal mechanisms influence stability and accountability.

topics.title: The civil service: Keeping government working between elections
takeaways: Public service institutions implement government decisions.
Appointment and oversight rules affect professionalism.
Constitutional design can support inclusion and accountability.

topics.title: Comparative politics: Reading an electoral dataset critically
takeaways: Definitions determine which systems can be compared.
Check the date and sources behind an entry.
Institutional classifications need political and historical context.

topics.title: Dopamine: prediction error, learning and why “pleasure chemical” is too simple
takeaways: A dopamine burst tracks the gap between what was predicted and what happened, not the size of the pleasure.
A fully predicted reward produces no burst; an expected reward that fails to arrive produces a dip.
Wanting (motivation and effort) and liking (hedonic pleasure) depend on partly separate systems, which is why “pleasure chemical” misleads.
Different striatal territories carry different dopamine signals, so there is no single dopamine message.
Recent reviews argue prediction error alone cannot explain everything dopamine does — the theory is still moving.

topics.title: Muscle hypertrophy: what actually makes skeletal muscle grow?
takeaways: Mechanical tension in sets taken close to failure is the primary growth stimulus.
Each session lifts muscle protein synthesis temporarily; growth is the accumulation of many of these episodes.
Weekly hard sets and progressive overload matter far more than the choice of exercise or split.
Soreness measures disruption, not growth — it is a poor training guide.
Protein intake and sleep permit the adaptation; they never replace the stimulus.

topics.title: Creatine: ATP buffering, muscle performance and disputed brain claims
takeaways: Phosphocreatine is a rapid buffer that rebuilds ATP faster than glycolysis or oxidative metabolism can.
Supplementation raises muscle creatine stores by roughly a fifth, improving repeated high-intensity efforts and training volume.
Early weight gain is largely water drawn into muscle cells, not new tissue.
Brain creatine rises only slightly after supplementation, and cognitive results are mixed.
The strongest candidate cognitive effects are in stressed states such as sleep deprivation or hypoxia, and still need better-designed trials — general “brain benefit” claims outrun the evidence.

topics.title: How collagen is synthesized inside the body
takeaways: Hydroxylation of proline and lysine happens in the endoplasmic reticulum, before the helix can form.
Prolyl hydroxylase depends on vitamin C — the biochemistry behind scurvy's failing connective tissue.
Three chains coil into a triple helix; procollagen is secreted before its terminal propeptides are cleaved.
Lysyl oxidase then forms covalent cross-links, which give mature fibrils their tensile strength.
Eaten collagen is digested to amino acids and peptides; it supplies raw material and does not bypass this pathway.

topics.title: The glymphatic system: how the brain cleans itself
takeaways: Fluid moves along perivascular spaces and exchanges with the fluid between brain cells, carrying solutes toward lymphatic exits.
Human imaging shows cerebrospinal fluid pulsing in time with slow waves during sleep, which is genuine human evidence for a sleep-linked fluid rhythm.
Whether flow, rather than diffusion, drives solute movement through the tissue is actively disputed in the peer-reviewed literature.
No causal role for glymphatic failure in human Alzheimer's disease has been established, including by researchers who founded the field.
Sleep plainly matters for brain health; the precise plumbing remains an open question rather than settled fact.

topics.title: How banks create money when they lend
takeaways: Lending creates a matching deposit: both sides of the bank's balance sheet expand at the same instant.
Banks are not pure intermediaries passing savers' money to borrowers.
The textbook reserve multiplier does not describe modern banking; central banks steer interest rates, not a quantity of loans.
Repaying a loan destroys the deposit again, so the money stock shrinks as well as grows.
Real constraints are capital and liquidity rules, credit risk, profitability and competition for deposits.

topics.title: Why do onions make us cry?
takeaways: Onion cells store sulfur-containing amino acid sulfoxides apart from the enzyme alliinase.
Cutting ruptures cells; alliinase produces a sulfenic acid intermediate in moments.
Lachrymatory-factor synthase converts that intermediate into the volatile syn-propanethial S-oxide — the actual tear gas.
The gas reaches the cornea, irritates sensory nerves and provokes reflex tearing.
Silencing the lachrymatory-factor synthase gene yields tearless onions, but also shifts the plant's flavour chemistry.

topics.title: How octopuses think with their arms
takeaways: The majority of an octopus's neurons lie in its arms rather than its central brain.
Each arm's axial nerve cord is segmented, with a spatial map of that arm's suckers.
Local circuits run reflexes and motor programmes, so a detached arm still produces coordinated movement.
Suckers sense chemically as well as mechanically — the arm effectively tastes by touch.
This distributed, embodied control of a soft body is a leading model for soft robotics.

topics.title: Why Renaissance perspective changed painting forever
takeaways: Brunelleschi's mirror experiment showed a geometric construction could convincingly imitate seen space.
Alberti's On Painting (1435) codified the method so any trained painter could build it.
A single vanishing point fixes the beholder's position, making the viewer part of the picture.
Measurable space let painters stage narrative: figures, architecture and light in proportional relation.
The convention became Europe's default pictorial space until it was deliberately broken in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.

topics.title: What makes a company tax resident in a country?
takeaways: No universal rule exists: incorporation, central management and control, or a combination, depending on the country.
“Central management and control” or “place of effective management” asks where strategic decisions are genuinely taken, not where documents are filed.
Dual residence is possible; treaties decide, and under the 2017 OECD Model this is normally settled by agreement between the tax authorities rather than an automatic formula.
Residence drives worldwide taxation, withholding rates and treaty access, so the consequences are substantial.
Outcomes turn on evidence — board minutes, where directors actually sit, who really decides — and on the particular jurisdictions concerned; this is context for understanding, not advice.

topics.title: Endocrine disruptors: how chemicals can imitate hormones
takeaways: Disruption can occur through receptor mimicry, blocking or changes in hormone metabolism.
Timing of exposure, such as during development, can matter as much as dose.
Regulation differs by jurisdiction and by substance, and scientific assessments are ongoing.

topics.title: RNA splicing: how one gene can make different proteins
takeaways: Introns are removed and exons joined before RNA is used to build protein.
Alternative splicing multiplies protein diversity beyond the number of genes.
Some therapies now target splicing, such as treatments for spinal muscular atrophy.

topics.title: Your microbiome is a chemical factory
takeaways: Fibre fermentation produces short-chain fatty acids used by gut cells and the body.
Gut microbes can change how some drugs and bile acids behave.
Composition varies widely between people, so a single "healthy microbiome" is hard to define.

topics.title: Stablecoins: what actually keeps a digital dollar worth $1?
takeaways: The peg is held by arbitrage and the credible promise of redemption.
Reserve quality, transparency and legal claims on reserves determine resilience.
Rules for stablecoin issuers differ by jurisdiction and have been changing.

topics.title: How a semiconductor is actually made
takeaways: Photolithography transfers circuit patterns onto the wafer, one layer at a time.
Doping changes silicon's conductivity to create transistors.
Few firms can produce leading-edge chips, making supply chains geopolitically sensitive.

topics.title: The internet is mostly physical: undersea cables
takeaways: Undersea fibre carries the large majority of data between continents.
Cables are thin in deep water and armoured near shore where damage risk is higher.
Redundant routes let traffic reroute when a cable is cut.

topics.title: How recommendation algorithms decide what you see
takeaways: Most systems predict engagement from past behaviour of you and similar people.
The optimisation target matters: time spent is not the same as satisfaction.
Some laws, such as the EU Digital Services Act, now require explanations of recommender systems.

topics.title: How do we prove an image or video is real in the AI era?
takeaways: Provenance records say where content came from; detection tries to infer it afterwards.
Watermarks and metadata can be removed or lost when files are re-shared.
Verification combines technical signals with journalism-style source checks.

topics.title: Dark patterns: when interface design manipulates your decisions
takeaways: Dark patterns work by adding friction to some choices and removing it from others.
Common types include confirm-shaming, hidden costs and subscription traps.
Whether a design is illegal depends on the jurisdiction and specific rules.

topics.title: Why monopolies emerge naturally in some digital markets
takeaways: Network effects make a service more valuable as more people use it.
Low marginal costs and data advantages reinforce scale.
Rules such as the EU Digital Markets Act target large "gatekeeper" platforms.

topics.title: mTOR vs AMPK: your body's growth and energy switches
takeaways: mTOR promotes building (protein synthesis, growth); AMPK promotes saving and refuelling.
AMPK can inhibit mTOR signalling, so the two act like a seesaw rather than independent dials.
Much research on these pathways comes from cells and animals; claims about lifespan or supplements in humans remain far less certain.

topics.title: How insurance companies insure disasters bigger than themselves
takeaways: Pooling works for independent risks; catastrophes are correlated.
Reinsurance and catastrophe bonds transfer extreme losses to other balance sheets.
Where private cover becomes unaffordable, governments sometimes create backstop schemes.

topics.title: How proteins fold — and what happens when they don't
takeaways: Sequence largely determines shape, and shape determines function.
Chaperones and the proteasome form a quality-control system for folding errors.
Aggregation of misfolded proteins is associated with several neurodegenerative diseases, though cause and effect differ between conditions.

topics.title: Epigenetic clocks: can we measure biological age?
takeaways: Clocks are built from patterns of DNA methylation, not from a single "ageing gene".
Different clocks measure different things and can disagree for the same person.
Commercial tests exist, but individual results and anti-ageing claims should be read cautiously.

topics.title: The placebo and nocebo effect inside the brain
takeaways: Expectation, conditioning and the clinical ritual all contribute to placebo responses.
Nocebo effects mean warnings and beliefs about side effects can produce symptoms.
Placebo effects are real but limited, which is why trials compare treatments against placebo.

topics.title: The blood-brain barrier: what is allowed into your brain?
takeaways: The barrier is a property of specialised brain blood vessels, not a separate membrane.
Glucose and some amino acids cross via transporters; many large or charged molecules cannot.
The barrier can be weakened in inflammation, stroke and some diseases.

topics.title: Your skeleton is constantly destroying and rebuilding itself
takeaways: Osteoclasts resorb bone; osteoblasts build it.
Mechanical loading and hormones such as oestrogen and parathyroid hormone regulate the balance.
Osteoporosis reflects an imbalance in remodelling, not simply a lack of calcium.

topics.title: Lactate is not just “muscle waste”
takeaways: Lactate production lets glycolysis keep running when demand is high.
Lactate is a fuel and a raw material for making glucose in the liver.
Delayed muscle soreness the next day is not caused by leftover lactate.

topics.title: How your body adapts to extreme heat
takeaways: Evaporation of sweat is the main cooling route in hot environments.
Acclimatisation develops over days and fades after weeks without exposure.
Heat stroke is a medical emergency in which body temperature regulation fails.

topics.title: The fall of the Roman Republic
takeaways: The Republic's decline was a long process, not a single event.
Personal armies and repeated civil wars eroded constitutional limits.
Augustus preserved republican appearances while creating a monarchy in practice.

topics.title: The Dutch East India Company: the world’s first mega-corporation?
takeaways: The VOC combined a trading business with state-like powers.
Its tradable shares helped develop early stock markets.
Its history includes forced labour and massacres as well as commercial innovation.

topics.title: The Magna Carta: what it actually changed
takeaways: The original 1215 charter failed quickly and led to civil war.
Its lasting influence came largely through later reissues and reinterpretation.
Most clauses are long obsolete; only a handful remain in English law.

topics.title: How Versailles controlled the French nobility
takeaways: Access to the king and court rituals became a currency of status.
Nobles living at court had less opportunity to build independent power.
The costs of Versailles and court life became a target of later criticism.

topics.title: The Black Death and how it transformed European society
takeaways: The disease spread along trade routes from Central Asia and the Black Sea.
Labour scarcity shifted bargaining power toward workers in some regions.
Mortality estimates vary by region and remain debated.

topics.title: The Cuban Missile Crisis — day by day
takeaways: The crisis ran from 16 to 28 October 1962.
A blockade was chosen over an immediate air strike.
A direct hotline between Washington and Moscow was set up afterwards.

topics.title: The Industrial Revolution from the worker’s point of view
takeaways: Factory work replaced much home-based production.
Historians debate when living standards for ordinary workers began to improve clearly.
Factory Acts from 1833 onward began restricting child labour in Britain.

topics.title: The Green Revolution
takeaways: High-yield varieties needed fertiliser and water to perform.
Cereal production grew faster than population in many developing countries.
Critics point to soil, water and biodiversity impacts and inequality.

topics.title: How propaganda worked during the Cold War
takeaways: Broadcasting across borders was a central tool.
Culture, sport and science were used as symbols of each system's success.
Some Western cultural programmes were secretly funded by intelligence agencies.

topics.title: Why cities built walls — and why they stopped
takeaways: Walls served for defence, taxation and control of movement.
Cannon led to the star-shaped bastion fort from the fifteenth century on.
Vienna's Ringstrasse replaced the city's old fortifications.

topics.title: The Thirty Years’ War and the making of the modern state system
takeaways: The war combined Catholic–Protestant conflict with dynastic power politics.
Parts of Germany lost a large share of their population.
The "Westphalian sovereignty" idea owes much to later interpretation.

topics.title: The Scramble for Africa
takeaways: By 1914 only Ethiopia and Liberia remained independent.
The Berlin Conference regulated European claims rather than dividing the whole map at once.
Colonial rule relied on violence, extraction and indirect rule through local elites.

topics.title: How universal suffrage gradually emerged
takeaways: Suffrage expanded in stages rather than all at once.
Women's suffrage movements used petitions, protest and civil disobedience.
Formal rights and real access to voting did not always coincide.

topics.title: The Opium Wars
takeaways: The trade imbalance over tea drove the opium business.
The Treaty of Nanjing (1842) ceded Hong Kong Island and opened treaty ports.
The wars weakened Qing authority and shaped modern Chinese nationalism.

topics.title: The South Sea Bubble of 1720
takeaways: The scheme tied a debt conversion to a speculative share price.
Prices rose far beyond any plausible trading profits before collapsing.
A similar bubble, the Mississippi scheme, occurred in France at the same time.

topics.title: The Nuremberg Trials and the birth of modern international criminal law
takeaways: The trials charged individuals, not states.
"Crimes against humanity" was prosecuted by an international court for the first time.
Critics noted it was victors' justice, since Allied conduct was not tried.

topics.title: How the Ottoman Empire governed such a diverse territory
takeaways: Religious communities managed matters like marriage and education internally.
The devshirme system recruited Christian boys into the army and administration for a period.
Nineteenth-century Tanzimat reforms tried to modernise and centralise the state.

topics.title: Salt as a political weapon
takeaways: Salt taxes hit the poor hardest because everyone needs salt.
The gabelle contributed to grievances before the French Revolution.
The Salt March showed how a simple act could mobilise mass resistance.

topics.title: The Haitian Revolution
takeaways: It is the only successful large-scale slave revolt that founded a state.
Napoleon's attempt to restore slavery failed militarily.
The 1825 indemnity demanded by France burdened Haiti's economy for generations.

topics.title: How the Medici built power through banking
takeaways: Banking for the papacy was a major source of Medici wealth.
Power came through patronage and alliances rather than official titles at first.
The bank itself declined and failed in the late fifteenth century.

topics.title: Why inflation can continue after the original shock is gone
takeaways: Second-round effects spread an initial shock through wages and prices.
Expectations matter because they are built into price and wage setting.
Economists debate how strong wage–price spirals are in practice.

topics.title: Why some countries stay poor while others grow
takeaways: Institutions shape incentives to invest and innovate.
Health, education and infrastructure support productivity.
No single policy formula explains every growth success.

topics.title: What actually causes inequality
takeaways: Wealth is usually far more unequally distributed than income.
Taxes and transfers significantly reduce measured income inequality in many countries.
Explanations are debated, and several causes typically act together.

topics.title: Why CEOs and top workers earn so much more than others
takeaways: Pay tied to company size and share price can grow very quickly.
Winner-take-most markets reward the top performers disproportionately.
Governance and disclosure rules influence executive pay.

topics.title: Why prices are not simply “cost + profit”
takeaways: Willingness to pay drives pricing as much as cost.
Price elasticity describes how demand changes when prices move.
Market power lets firms price further above cost.

topics.title: Price discrimination: why everyone pays a different price for the same thing
takeaways: Firms segment customers by time, group, quantity or version.
Resale must be difficult for discrimination to work.
Some forms are restricted by consumer or competition law.

topics.title: Behavioral economics: why humans systematically make “irrational” choices
takeaways: Losses tend to weigh more heavily than equivalent gains.
Defaults strongly shape outcomes because people often stick with them.
Not every popular behavioural effect has held up in replication.

topics.title: Network effects: why some markets tip toward one winner
takeaways: Direct effects come from users; indirect effects come from complementary sides.
Tipping can make early leads self-reinforcing.
Interoperability can weaken winner-take-all dynamics.

topics.title: How supply chains transmit economic shocks
takeaways: Just-in-time systems save costs but reduce buffers.
Single-source components create critical vulnerabilities.
Firms and governments now weigh resilience against efficiency.

topics.title: Why minimum wages do not always behave like simple supply-and-demand diagrams predict
takeaways: Monopsony power can mean a minimum wage raises pay without cutting jobs.
Firms can adjust through prices, turnover or hours.
Evidence is strongest for moderate increases.

topics.title: Why central banks need credibility
takeaways: Expectations make credibility self-reinforcing.
Many central banks target inflation around 2%.
Political pressure on central banks can undermine credibility.

topics.title: How financial crises actually spread
takeaways: Short-term funding makes institutions vulnerable to runs.
Fire sales spread losses to others holding similar assets.
Central banks act as lenders of last resort in panics.

topics.title: Why interest rates affect almost everything
takeaways: Higher rates raise borrowing costs and reward saving.
Asset prices tend to fall when the discount rate used to value them rises.
Monetary policy effects arrive with variable lags, often over a year or more.

topics.title: Why currencies rise and fall
takeaways: Higher interest rates can attract capital and strengthen a currency.
Purchasing power parity describes a long-run tendency, not a short-run rule.
Some countries fix or manage their currency instead of letting it float.

topics.title: Why housing becomes unaffordable
takeaways: Supply restrictions in high-demand cities are a major driver.
Lower interest rates raise how much buyers can borrow and bid.
Affordability depends on both prices and financing costs.

topics.title: Why governments can borrow so much money
takeaways: Debt sustainability depends on interest rates, growth and budget balance together.
Government bonds are a core safe asset for banks and investors.
Debt crises tend to hit countries borrowing in currencies they cannot issue.

topics.title: Yield curves: why the shape of interest rates matters
takeaways: The curve reflects expected future policy rates plus a term premium.
An inverted curve suggests markets expect rates to fall.
Inversions have preceded many recessions but timing varies widely.

topics.title: Why companies are worth the present value of future cash flows
takeaways: A euro in the future is worth less than a euro today.
Riskier cash flows are discounted at higher rates.
Valuations are highly sensitive to long-term growth assumptions.

topics.title: Why productivity determines long-term living standards
takeaways: Wages over time track productivity at the economy-wide level, though not always evenly.
Technology, education and investment are key drivers.
Many advanced economies have seen slower productivity growth since the mid-2000s.

topics.title: Why rice cultures and wheat cultures developed differently
takeaways: The hypothesis links farming demands to social habits.
Studies within China aimed to limit national differences as confounds.
Critics question the size and causal interpretation of the effects.

topics.title: The culture of cafés and why they became intellectual spaces
takeaways: Coffeehouses offered a cheap place to meet and talk.
Some became hubs for news, trade and insurance.
The "public sphere" idea is linked to Jürgen Habermas.

topics.title: Why some societies value minimalism and others ornament
takeaways: Aesthetic preferences carry moral and religious meanings.
Ornament can display craftsmanship and wealth.
Modernism reacted against nineteenth-century decoration.

topics.title: Why marriage means such different things across societies
takeaways: Marriage has often linked families and property.
Love marriage became an ideal relatively recently in many societies.
Legal recognition of marriage varies between jurisdictions.

topics.title: How cultures define childhood differently
takeaways: Childhood as a protected stage has expanded with schooling.
Parenting practices vary widely across cultures.
Legal ages for adulthood differ between countries.

topics.title: How food becomes national identity
takeaways: National cuisines are often constructed or standardised recently.
Migration shapes what countries eat.
Culinary heritage can become a diplomatic and economic tool.

topics.title: Why silence means different things in different cultures
takeaways: Pauses carry different meanings across cultures.
Communication styles vary in how much is said explicitly.
Individual differences exist within any culture.

topics.title: Why cultures experience time differently
takeaways: Punctuality norms vary widely.
Some cultures prioritise schedules; others relationships.
Industrialisation spread clock-based time discipline.

topics.title: Why people behave differently in public and private
takeaways: Social norms have more force in public.
Impression management shapes behaviour.
Online spaces blur public and private boundaries.

topics.title: The cultural history of cleanliness
takeaways: Hygiene norms have changed markedly over time.
Germ theory reshaped public health and personal habits.
Cleanliness has also been used as a marker of class and respectability.

topics.title: Why embarrassment and shame are cultural emotions
takeaways: Self-conscious emotions depend on social norms.
Shame targets the self; guilt targets a specific act.
Cultures differ in how these emotions are expressed and used.

topics.title: Why clothes communicate status before we even speak
takeaways: Clothes act as visible, costly signals of identity.
Sumptuary laws once regulated who could wear what.
Status signals shift when they become widely available.

topics.title: How cities create their own cultures
takeaways: Density enables specialised communities and scenes.
Migration brings new cultural influences to cities.
Urban cultures differ from rural ones in many measurable ways.

topics.title: How beauty standards change across time and place
takeaways: Some preferences are widespread; many are culturally specific.
Beauty ideals often signal status or wealth in their time.
Global media has increased the spread of particular standards.

topics.title: Why table manners are so different around the world
takeaways: Manners signal respect and belonging within a group.
Rules often reflect local food and tools.
What is polite in one culture can be rude in another.

topics.title: Why humans create rituals
takeaways: Rites of passage mark changes in social status.
Shared rituals can increase group cohesion.
Personal rituals may help manage anxiety before stressful events.

topics.title: Why every culture has ghosts
takeaways: Ghost beliefs connect to ideas about death and the afterlife.
The mind readily attributes ambiguous sounds and shapes to agents.
Many cultures honour ancestors through regular rituals.

topics.title: How language changes the way people think
takeaways: Strong linguistic determinism is not supported.
Weaker influences on perception and memory have evidence.
Effects are debated and often modest.

topics.title: Why luxury exists in every society
takeaways: Luxury signals status and taste.
Rarity and price can increase desirability.
Definitions of luxury change over time and place.

topics.title: Why homes look so different across cultures
takeaways: Climate and materials strongly influence architecture.
Family and social structures shape room layouts.
Vernacular architecture adapts to local conditions.

topics.title: Different sizes of infinity
takeaways: Two sets have the same size if their elements can be paired one to one.
The diagonal argument shows the real numbers are uncountable.
The continuum hypothesis is independent of standard set theory.

topics.title: Bayes’ theorem: how evidence should change your beliefs
takeaways: Base rates strongly affect conclusions.
Evidence updates beliefs rather than replacing them.
Ignoring base rates is a common reasoning error.

topics.title: The mathematics of optimal decisions
takeaways: Expected value weighs outcomes by their probabilities.
Optimal stopping gives rules for when to stop searching.
Assumptions strongly determine the "optimal" answer.

topics.title: Game theory: why rational people sometimes make bad collective choices
takeaways: A Nash equilibrium is where no player gains by changing alone.
Individual rationality can produce collective harm.
Repetition and reputation can sustain cooperation.

topics.title: How queueing theory explains waiting lines
takeaways: Waits rise steeply as utilisation nears 100%.
Variability in arrivals and service increases queues.
A single shared queue is often fairer and more efficient than many separate ones.

topics.title: Network mathematics: why some people and websites become hubs
takeaways: Preferential attachment explains hub formation.
Many networks are "small worlds" with short paths.
Removing hubs can fragment a network.

topics.title: The mathematics of epidemics
takeaways: R0 above 1 means an outbreak can grow.
Interventions aim to push the effective reproduction number below 1.
Real models add behaviour, networks and uncertainty.

topics.title: Why averages can lie
takeaways: Means are sensitive to extreme values.
Medians often describe typical values better.
Aggregated data can hide or reverse subgroup patterns.

topics.title: Why the normal distribution appears everywhere
takeaways: The central limit theorem explains the bell curve.
Normal data cluster symmetrically around the mean.
Assuming normality for heavy-tailed data underestimates extremes.

topics.title: Non-Euclidean geometry
takeaways: On a sphere, triangle angles add up to more than 180°.
Hyperbolic geometry allows infinitely many parallels.
General relativity relies on curved geometry.

topics.title: Gödel’s incompleteness theorem
takeaways: Some true arithmetic statements are unprovable within a given system.
A system cannot prove its own consistency.
The theorems are often misapplied outside formal systems.

topics.title: Why randomness is so unintuitive
takeaways: Truly random sequences contain streaks.
Independent events have no memory.
